final.title: What subscription sprawl is really hiding
final.body:
Subscription sprawl usually looks like a cost problem, but in a small business it often hides a workflow problem. The real question is not which tool to cancel. It is which subscription exists because someone is still doing part of the work by hand.

A useful first pass is simple: list every tool, what it is used for, how often it is actually touched, and what recurring task would stop if it disappeared. Then separate active dependencies from legacy extras. Often the monthly fee is not the main cost; the hidden cost is owner time wrapped around manual steps.

The decision boundary is one repeatable workflow. Example only: emails arrive, data is copied into a CRM, and a second tool is used to chase the next step. If that pattern repeats at least weekly, produces a measurable outcome, and stays outside excluded work like medical, legal, high-sensitivity financial, bulk cold email, scan-heavy OCR-dependent, or unsupported compliance work, it may be worth asking whether a bounded automation fits. The question is not whether to automate everything. It is whether one specific workflow is worth diagnosing.

Bareni is a one-person consulting practice being built inside the customer’s environment. Finished code and customer-named accounts are handed over as policy and no-lock-in positioning, while human approval stays in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions. That part should stay boring.

For a founder, the next step is to write down one recurring workflow and decide whether you want to keep paying for software, keep paying for manual work, or test a small automation instead.
